slides.title: Hyperscale is transforming civilization
slides.subtitle: Let’s make it work for all of us
slides.body: A hyperscale data center is a massive data center engineered for large-scale workloads, with at least 5,000 servers. By IDC’s definition, a hyperscaler runs 5,000 servers or more on at least 10,000 square feet. The International Energy Agency sorts data centers into three kinds: enterprise, colocation and service provider, and hyperscale. Efficient hyperscale data centers spend about 7 percent of their electricity on cooling, against more than 30 percent for less efficient enterprise data centers. All three kinds are adding to the growth in electricity use.

slides.title: Where the computing lives
slides.subtitle: Data centers, and the AI campuses among them
slides.body: PeeringDB places 5,274 data centers in 148 countries on the map. Epoch’s record of GPU clusters adds 398 more AI sites; 188 are in China, where Epoch names the country but not the site, so they are not plotted. Seen from afar, each country shows its count; up close, each point is a data center. The magenta discs are AI compute, sized by its chips; the rings are AI campuses still being built.

slides.title: Who keeps the lights on
slides.subtitle: The power partners behind the campuses
slides.body: Each campus has a counterpart in the power sector, by contract or by proximity. Constellation sells Microsoft the output of the restarted Three Mile Island reactor; Entergy Louisiana is building the gas plants for Meta at Hyperion. The yellow lines run from plant to campus.

slides.title: Where the cables cross

Fossil fuels make 87 percent of Egypt’s electricity, and solar and wind 7 percent. The bright lines are the Europe-to-Asia cable systems that cross Egypt.

slides.body: Data centers accounted for about 560 billion litres of water consumption in 2023 in the IEA’s accounting, which counts the water behind their electricity as well as on-site cooling, rising toward 1,200 billion litres by 2030.
